back: Shaping a material by removing parts of it — cutting, drilling, sawing, filing or machining.
Shaping or building a product by adding material or joining parts — 3D printing, welding, gluing, screwing.
A straight reference edge that all measurements are marked out from.
A device that holds the work and/or guides the tool so an operation can be repeated accurately without marking out each part.
A solid shape that material is bent, laminated or formed around so every part takes the same shape.
Faster production, fewer mistakes and less waste, and interchangeable parts — essential for batch production.
A small hole drilled first to guide a screw or larger drill and stop timber splitting.
A hole just larger than the screw or bolt so it passes through without its thread gripping, pulling the parts together.
A hole drilled to the right size for a thread to be cut inside it with a tap — e.g. 5 mm for an M6 thread.
Countersunk: cone-shaped recess so a screw head sits flush. Counterbored: flat-bottomed recess so a bolt head sits below the surface.
A tap cuts an internal thread in a hole (taper, second, then plug tap); a die cuts an external thread on a rod.
Deforming changes shape without removing or adding material (bending, pressing). Reforming melts or softens it into a new shape (casting, moulding).
Permanent joining of metals with a lower-melting filler metal — soft solder for electronics and plumbing, silver solder for jewellery. Flux keeps the joint clean.
Permanent fixing where the rivet is deformed to clamp parts. Pop rivets are fitted from one side with a rivet gun.
A wastage process where the work spins and a cutting tool removes material to make round parts — cylinders, tapers, grooves.
Both ends cut at 45° to form a neat 90° corner with no end grain showing — weak unless reinforced. Used for picture frames.
Round wooden pegs glued into matching holes in both parts — strong and hidden; a dowelling jig lines up the holes.
Butt: one end glued against the other face — quick but weakest. Lap: one piece sits in a rebate — larger gluing area, so stronger.
PVC — it gives off toxic fumes.
Solvent cement (e.g. Tensol for acrylic), epoxy resin and plastic welding.
Nuts and bolts, self-tapping screws into moulded bosses, snap fits and clips, hinges and knock-down fittings.
Adhesive for wood, boards, paper and card. Dries clear; joints must be clamped while it sets.
Spread on both surfaces, left touch-dry, then pressed together — bonds instantly. For laminates, rubber, leather and fabric.
Two-part (resin + hardener) adhesive that bonds almost anything, including different materials. Strong, waterproof, gap-filling but slow and expensive.
Die casting, sand casting, press forming and stamping, extrusion and CNC machining.
Injection moulding, blow moulding, vacuum forming and extrusion.
